items.question: How do you assess whether strong benchmark performance means a model has actually solved a task?
items.object: Benchmark performance as evidence that a model has solved a task
items.answer: We measure performance on a benchmark. And if that's all we care about, it seems like we can do really well because if you collect data that looks like the data you want to do well on, you can just throw a lot of compute at it. But does that actually solve the task if we just test it in a slightly different way that is also meaningful from a deployment perspective? When does that break the models, and why does that happen? How do the training dynamics or the data curation, what aspects of these actually influence this behavior, and what's the right way to intervene and make these problems go away?

items.question: What drew you to studying the failures of highly capable deep learning models?
items.object: The failures of highly capable deep learning models
items.answer:
In my undergrad, I was always excited by complexity theory, and I really liked the elegance of thinking about what's possible and what's not. But at the same time, like several others, I also had the itch to work in something that had immediate impact, was practical. When I started doing research, around 2015, 2016, deep learning was really taking off. This was post-ImageNet and so on, and naturally I got excited about it.

The moments that shaped my thinking around this were when I was at Stanford. I was attending a couple of talks, and one of them was on adversarial examples, which showed me how these really capable models can also fail in spectacularly surprising and maybe seemingly dumb ways. They also had some immediate practical questions around security, reliability in the wild, and so on.

That's sort of what got me thinking about how do we think about these really capable systems that also have these failures. It also tied into my itch on complexity and thinking about abstractions and making precise statements about these things. It kind of felt like a nice combination, because a lot of these aspects cannot be captured by just specific numbers and a benchmark, and really need to go one step beyond to think about what these models learn, when do they work, when do they fail, and so on.

items.question: How do you use distribution shifts to frame your research into whether models actually solve the tasks measured by benchmarks?

items.question: How do you think about whether more pre-training makes a model better for downstream use?
items.object: The effect of additional pre-training on downstream model usefulness
items.answer:
We realized the answer is really no. For a lot of things, actually, model performance on benchmarks kind of tracks performance, including reliability or robustness to a lot of distribution shifts. What we found, what the community has found, is in general the more data you train on, all of these numbers go up. But this one aspect of how easy it is to adapt these models after you train them on data, we actually found the reverse thing happens at some point.

If you take a small model and keep training on it on a lot of data, we see that eventually the model that has been trained on more data, that you've thrown more compute on, is worse as a starting point for fine-tuning than an earlier checkpoint that you had. This was a really striking result because it's one of the first realistic cases where more compute in a very non-contrived setting, on high-quality data, is actually making a model worse. It's not just that it saturates, but it's actively worse.

Another context in which this happens is when people are trying to serve quantized models to improve efficiency. There also we find this kind of trend where, as you throw more data at these models and then you quantize them, the model trained with more data is still better, but then you see this U-curve where at some point showing more data actually means that this model is worse after quantizing. That's again a case where your downstream model is strictly worse, even though you've spent more compute with the best of intentions and shown good data.

I think this was a really interesting finding that people should think more about. One important aspect of using these models is fine-tuning and adapting, and our current push toward improving this pre-training, or the first step of this process, by really optimizing that doesn't mean it's going to be good after doing your fine-tuning or post-training.

This is not just a theoretical limit. We actually see that a lot of people talk about how Llama 3—this is before the Llama 4 release, so people were just talking about Llama 3 versus Llama 2—and a lot of people found that Llama 3 was much harder to fine-tune. Academics regularly fine-tune models, and this was sort of Graham's question too. It ties into this idea that because we have trained on so much data, at some point Llama 3 is still really good at benchmarks, but it's just worse if you want to use it for your task.

Similarly, we ran experiments on the M O checkpoints, because they're releasing all these checkpoints so we can do analysis on them, and we found that the smallest size model, 1B, I believe, that was trained on three trillion tokens is actually worse than the model that was trained on fewer tokens after we do this kind of fine-tuning or post-training on very realistic benchmarks that people care about. This was an exciting result that shows that one axis of rethinking pre-training is: how do we get a good starting point for fine-tuning?

items.question: How do you characterize the relationship between pre-training token count and model size in your precision and fine-tuning results?
items.object: The relationship between pre-training token count and model size in precision and fine-tuning results
items.answer: For the precision result, that's exactly what we found. We tried different exponents, but it turns out that in our experiments the exponents turned out to be the same. So it's literally the ratio. But in our fine-tuning, we didn't do precise curves because a lot of them depends on the exact distribution of interest. There's no clean mathematical result, or the trend won't be the same for all datasets. In general, we find that a larger model can take in more tokens before it shows the inverse effect compared to a small model. In some sense, a larger model can absorb more tokens efficiently, but it's not always exactly the ratio. It could be a different exponent.

items.question: How do you think the relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning distributions affects catastrophic overtraining?
items.object: The relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning distributions in catastrophic overtraining
items.answer: There are different ways to think about this. One is purely: is the model more stable, in that it can move in different directions without losing too much? And so that's this token-to-parameter kind of thing, which could roughly correspond to that. The other question is how much do we actually need to move? We have some experiments in our catastrophic overtraining ICML paper where one proxy for how much to move is just the learning rate. If the model gets good performance even with a small learning rate, then that roughly means the model hasn't moved too much, and it kind of works like the distribution is closer in some sense. We do find some interesting trends over there as well. If we start measuring or fine-tuning on things that are very close, then we actually don't see this effect. The models are able to take in more tokens and still show good performance because we don't really end up moving the model much. In the limit, if the fine-tuning matches pre-training, then we just get back the usual: things go down as we show more data. But then as we have larger changes, these kinds of trends start happening where at some point the model is actually getting worse. One challenge is that it's not very easy to say which distributions are close or hard, because we might have some intuition for what this is, but how the model stores information might be different, which is why we look at learning rate itself as a proxy for how much the model changes, as a way of saying how different the distributions are.

items.question: How do you understand the point at which additional pre-training data starts hurting a model’s fine-tuning performance?
items.object: The point at which additional pre-training data begins to hurt fine-tuning performance
items.answer:
I guess what actually happens is at some point, overall, there is a regime where showing more data does help, no matter what the model size, because the model is just learning stuff. Then at some point the model gets so brittle that whatever it learns from the more data is overcome by its brittleness, and so we start seeing this jump. There is a point where more data starts hurting you, so it's a U-shaped kind of situation. The point at which this U is really depends on, like we discussed, the data that you're fine-tuning on.

We are able to characterize these precisely in the quantization setting because there's just fewer factors to account for, because you just add noise. In this fine-tuning setting it's a little bit more tricky because we can't exactly say what the distribution of interest is. But if we fix a certain distribution or a certain learning rate that we care about, then again this point actually becomes predictable. We didn't go into modeling this functional form too carefully in the fine-tuning setting in our paper, and I think that would be very interesting future work, once we decide what kind of distributions you want to fine-tune on and make decisions on how to allocate compute and do the scaling laws and so on. But we do see trends where it feels fairly predictable with a nice mathematical form.

items.question: How would you use your findings on overtraining to choose a base model for fine-tuning?
items.object: Base model selection for fine-tuning
items.answer:
I think if you are using a 1 billion model size, which again you might want to use for efficiency reasons, if it's trained beyond 2.5 trillion tokens or maybe even two trillion tokens, because we didn't have too much granularity in the public checkpoints, I would say maybe that's a point where you don't want to use that model unless you're sure that you don't want to change the model too much.

In terms of the gray areas in between, I think we do have to do some preliminary experiments where we take a bunch of different checkpoints and see what the fine-tuning performance actually ends up looking like. That would give us some sense of which part of the U-curve we're on. The understanding it gives us is that we expect this shape, and we can try to probe to see which regime current models are in. That would guide us to where the optimal could be.

items.question: How do you think about the challenges of unlearning harmful knowledge or private information as a safety use case of fine-tuning language models?
items.object: Unlearning harmful knowledge or private information from language models
items.answer: When I think about the use cases of fine-tuning, one is to specialize and push a few numbers on your use case rather than the benchmark. But another important use case for post-training or fine-tuning methodologies is safety. A lot of the alignment work is trying to teach the model post hoc what is good and what's bad. Similarly, we might try to unlearn harmful knowledge or private information. That's a very safety-specific use case of fine-tuning. We tried to look at why it's so hard to do unlearning in English. There are so many papers that are published, and it very much reminded me of adversarial examples from my PhD, where people had all these defense ideas, but then Carlini would break all of them. items.question: Why do you think existing methods for making language models forget information have had limited success?
items.object: Existing language-model unlearning methods
items.answer:
The first way to try to address this would be to fine-tune so that the model has high loss on all of these things that you want to forget. People realized that you can't actually do too well because then you have to really change everything a lot, and that destroys a lot of information in the model. Another idea is maybe this information could be localized, or maybe we can find specific neurons or subspaces and try to erase those parts. Even that has limited success for two reasons. One is we have to first find a way to figure out where those neurons are which store this information. Second, even after we find that, it's not clear what's the right way to erase that without destroying everything else.

The assumption here is that there exist such neurons in the first place. What we show is that that's actually not true. There's no reason in how we've trained these models that encourages or should allow this information to be disentangled in this nice way. It seems like maybe we see such separation, but because the separation is not very good, that's why our unlearning methods don't work very well.

items.question: How do you think language-model training should change to enable downstream unlearning through memorization sinks?
items.object: Memorization sinks and training models for downstream unlearning
items.answer:
Instead of constraining ourselves to work with this starting point that is not very good, in that it's not really disentangling all of these things, what if we had the flexibility to train our models in a way that enables this kind of downstream unlearning, because we know that that's a use case which we might care about?

That inspired this work on memorization sinks, which is taking the same idea or assumption that people implicitly tried to make about models—that maybe information is isolated to neurons—but instead of waiting for it to happen by magic, let's try to actually enforce that by design. We find in our paper, both through experiments and analysis, that normal training does not actually lead to this assumption being true. The main idea is we don't encourage or force this sort of disentanglement, and it really depends on the bias of the training algorithm. The current training algorithms don't have a bias to enable this kind of separation, but we can encourage the separation.

items.question: How do you think memorization sinks can separate document-specific information from knowledge shared across documents?
items.object: Memorization sinks
items.answer:

items.question: Where do you see room to improve your paper's approach to assigning documents their own neuron subspaces?
items.object: Document-specific neuron subspaces for isolating memorization during model training
items.answer:
What we do in our paper is, for every document, we have a hash or some kind of random neurons, and that particular combination of neurons is activated. This effectively models one direction in a high-dimensional space that's allotted to this new document.

One could consider smarter approaches; there might be improvements to this, like which layers should we look at. We only looked at the MLP layers, and we only introduced these things within the MLP layers, building on the intuition people had that facts or factual information is generally stored in the MLP layers. I could imagine there's a lot of research that one could do to be more intelligent about this. We could also try to have related documents share similar subspaces in some way. We could have a softer version of this where instead of everything being orthogonal, we can maybe put things that are slightly close together closer together. That might further push up performance.

I think there are a lot of things that one could do here, and I'm very excited about this because I think it tells us ways in which we can get more control over these models by design. It also makes me think about the overlap with the Anthropic circuit tracing work and if there's some way to combine these techniques to better localize concepts.

items.question: What led you to question LLMs' ability to generate creative ideas?
items.object: LLMs' ability to generate creative ideas
items.answer: I guess like every AI researcher, I try to use LLMs as much as I can to automate and make my life easy. Sometimes, you prompt the model to generate homework problems, especially because you want the model to generate something new. I'm like, “Can the model come up with something really clever, a way to test students that I couldn't come up with?” Or new research ideas to write some new grant proposals. I've almost always found that the models have never been able to give me something that's truly, “Aha, I hadn't thought of that.” They're great at almost every other task that I try to use them for. They're great at summarization. They're great at looking at what's common across a bunch of different things and drawing some stuff there. But they're not really good at these open-ended tasks that I give these models. That was sort of the motivation.

items.question: Why did you choose to study LLM creativity through first principles and simple tasks?
items.object: Studying LLM creativity through first principles and simple tasks
items.answer: There's also work that people have been trying to do in the community about analyzing research ideas, actually running human studies to see: can models generate ideas or not? There's been a lot of back and forth, so it's something that is very fuzzy and seems like something people are thinking about. This was in collaboration with Vishnav, who's a researcher at Google. We were having this conversation, and he was also an author on this next limitations of next token prediction paper. I wanted to do similar research: let's try to identify what are the core principles that we might need for creativity, and can we test whether that can emerge from the training objectives that we have for these models? That's a way we can get an answer to this, because having actual benchmarks and testing creativity, and who knows what's in the training data, all of that makes it harder to answer this at scale. items.question: How do you understand the effect of additional training on LLMs' ability to try diverse solutions?
items.object: The effect of additional training on diversity in LLM problem-solving
items.answer: I also had another project in my lab that looks at this from slightly more realistic settings of problem-solving, like reasoning. There again we found that models, especially after you train them more, started collapsing in their solutions. For people familiar with inference-time settings, you can either give the model one shot to answer or query it multiple times. What we find is that when we try to train models, in general their performance at this one-shot setting does go up, but they also get worse at the “give it multiple times” setting. When models are trained too much, it seems like they start giving the same solution and try the same incorrect thing rather than actually trying diverse solutions. I was convinced that this is a problem, and that models are not very good at trying out creative, diverse solutions, even on realistic tasks.

items.question: How do you make creativity concrete enough to study which training objectives might encourage it in language models?
items.object: Formalizing creativity to study language-model training objectives
items.answer:
We drew inspiration from a lot of work in cognitive science, particularly Bowden's work that tries to formalize some notions of creativity. We're in no way thinking about what's the right definition of creativity, but more like let's lean into the definitions that cognitive scientists have taken about creativity and use that.

A concrete example: there's this notion called combinational creativity, and I think a nice example of that is wordplay. The example is: why did the scarecrow win an award? The punchline is, “Because he was outstanding in his field.” If you think about why this is creative or funny, scarecrow and award are two seemingly different, unrelated words, but there is this actual connection—“outstanding”—that is somewhat novel or something that you hadn't thought about, that links these two words together.

That's an example of combinational creativity, where we're trying to see whether the model can find unexpected connections through a graph, or find two words that have a common parent, like the two different interpretations of “outstanding.” Can the model give new ways of doing this? The way we abstract this is: let's say we have a graph and we teach the model all the edges in the graph. Can the model discover new siblings, two nodes that have a parent? The two nodes don't look connected, but they have a parent. Can the model see some of these and then generate more of these? Can it find new connections in the graph? That's one example of creativity abstracted, following Bowden's work on combinational creativity. They have a lot of examples on how a lot of things that we do that we think are creative are actually finding these unexpected connections between things.

The other kind of creativity we consider is exploratory: we just want to free-form find interesting things in the world. Of course they still have some structure, but it's a latent structure. We want to find new things within that structure. Bowden explains that a lot of the work artists do, for example, is this kind of exploratory creativity. We try to write this down in math and symbols that we can train models on. Let's say we train on a bunch of circles, for example; can the model find new circles or new triangles in the graph that the model wasn't trained on?

These are the ways we think about creativity. They're not perfect by any means, but I think they capture some of these core principles, and they already show why certain training objectives might be good or bad for these notions of creativity. We can dig more into what's the right way to train these models, what could current training be missing, and how we should be thinking about new ways to pre-train these models to encourage this kind of creativity.

items.question: How do you distinguish the creativity you want from large language models from their ability to generate something new on request?
items.object: Open-ended creativity in large language models
items.answer:
I think one notion of creativity is just: is it generating something that's not in the training data, and something meaningful? This was for a long time not easy, and it's very impressive that models can do this and can generate poems in the style of blah blah blah. I think the difference becomes what I feel is open-ended versus closed-ended. In these cases, we're still roughly saying where we want to go. If I say, “Write X in the style of Y,” I'm telling the model what to do, and then the model can fill out the path.

What I'm thinking about with creativity is: take me to things that I've just never seen or thought of before. Our constructs, and even our own use of these models, are trying to say that's maybe where we want to think more. For another example, when I look into these benchmarks or people trying to use models, for example KernelBench, to solve index problems in new ways, it feels like we still have to carefully prompt the model on strategies or things it has already done and things it should explore. That part is still coming from our explicit instruction even though it's generating new things. I want to see: can they actually do this part on their own too? I think that's what it would mean to meaningfully go beyond what we are able to do and find new things. If we are able to do that at scale, then we're going to discover a lot of interesting new things and find new connections.

items.question: How do you understand language models’ difficulty generating jokes that connect unexpected entities?
items.object: Language models’ difficulty generating novel jokes and the limitations of their training
items.answer: We couldn't get one that obeys this structure of connecting unexpected entities. The prompt would be, for example, “Tell me a joke that's funny because it connects to unexpected entities,” and that was the kind of wordplay that we were trying to get at. It's finding a new connection that I hadn't thought about, but it was kind of bad at doing that. You could think of many different structures of jokes, but this particular aspect of the hidden punchline that the model discovered, it didn't. I think there's a very deep reason, which we explain in the paper: a lot of the training data doesn't have supervision on this. It doesn't say first the punchline and then the joke, so the model can do that. Instead, the punchline is latent, and that means the models are not able to learn the right structure. They end up learning some things local that are sort of memorization, and they don't learn this true process that we want, where you think of something, search over all possible things, find something new, and then generate them. That's the limitation that we try to show in the training of these models.

items.question: How do you think about the kind of creativity you want language models to exhibit?
items.object: Structured creativity in language models
items.answer:
A lot of creativity is not just simply saying something crazy, but we want it to be still structured and meaningful. If you think about use cases like molecular biology or drug discovery, it's not like we want to generate random new things. We want the model to infer the right latent structure and generate new things according to that structure. That's really the kind of creativity that I'm thinking about and that we try to model in these tasks.

Just crank up the temperature and you can start getting crazy things, but then the model is also going to be less structured. We really want this structured exploration from these models. Similarly, when I try to get a model to generate a homework problem, I don't want it to put together something meaningless. It's creative, but I really want it to follow some logic or some structure there.

items.question: Why do you think multi-token prediction and diffusion objectives are worth pursuing for language models that produce diverse generations?
items.object: Multi-token prediction and diffusion objectives for training language models
items.answer:
Another part that we show in the paper is actually different training objectives, like teacherless training. That could be things like multi-token prediction, where we are trying to discourage the model from getting the right answer by just looking locally. If it has to actually generate the entire pattern or the entire set of things, then that encourages the model to have this global understanding. People are excited about diffusion models lately. We find that diffusion models also have a similar thing where they don't show all the tokens and they mask out different things, and so that encourages the model to have some sort of planning, the ability to do more global things. We find these two objectives work a lot better in our experiments.

One is multi-token prediction, where we force a model to produce multiple tokens at a time rather than just one token, see the correct answer, and then the next token. In multi-token prediction, the model does not get that local supervision; it has to get everything right before it gets reward. Diffusion models can be thought of as having these different masks or different orderings, and that also encourages the model to have more global understanding. Both of those are alternatives that might be worth pursuing more seriously if we care about getting these kinds of diverse generations from the models.

items.question: How do you think randomness should be introduced into language models to produce diverse but structured generations?
items.object: Structured randomness for diverse language-model generations
items.answer:
There's an underexplored aspect of how to get diverse things from the model. Right now there are two ways. One is we think about the diverse stuff ourselves. When people prompt the models, we give more specific instructions, and then we're like, “Actually, I want to do something else,” and then we tell the model, “Go do this instead.” The other way machine learning people may be thinking about is just increase the temperature, and that gives you more tokens. Like I said earlier, that also tends to destroy the structure.

We try to think about how to elicit this randomness from the model that can be structured. One way that seemed more natural than temperature sampling is first generate a random idea for you, and then follow that idea and generate all your tokens. The right place to introduce randomness is probably at the beginning, where the model commits to exploring something. Once it decides to go down that path, if you keep increasing the temperature, it's just going to go all over the place. Instead, we pick something and then stick to it. At test time, if you want more diverse generations, we would sample new prefixes or new starting points and then let the model do its thing. That's where we're trying to say we should introduce randomness, which is the “roll the dice.” We roll the dice first, and then based on the outcome of the die, we pick that thought and go with it.

This requires training the model to be able to do that, and we have a very simple way to do this in the paper: in the training data, we have random prefixes that we prepend. The model conditions on a random prefix, and you can think of that as some proxy for a random idea, and then it generates things. At test time we can get new ideas or new generations from the model by changing this prefix.

items.question: Why do you see conditioning language models on different prefixes as a promising way to generate structured diversity?
items.object: Conditioning language models on random or meaningful prefixes to produce structured diversity
items.answer:
In our paper, because our experiments are so simple, a random nonsensical prefix actually just works, which is surprising. We don't really understand why it works; that's very interesting future work too. But as a proof of concept, it seems like there's maybe some meat here. What we are looking at now in my group is having more meaningful prefixes, which actually capture what exactly the idea is, some semantics of the idea, and then condition on that to generate things. If this paradigm of pre-training ends up working, this will also give us more controlled, diverse generations. Instead of prompting the model with explicit instructions, we can just change this prefix that we condition on in some nice way, and then we can get diversity in that sense as well.

That's what we are trying to say: maybe rather than doing temperature sampling, we can tell the model to condition on new ideas that can then be randomized or made more diverse. That way of training as well as inference might be a better way to get structured diversity from these models.

items.question: How do you think about achieving controlled diversity when language models generate parallel lines of thought at inference time?
items.object: Controlled diversity in language models' parallel lines of thought
items.answer:
It also depends on how these parallel thoughts are actually coming. I don't know how exactly those thoughts are being generated behind the scenes there.

If they're doing RL on a starting point, the question is: how can we leverage the starting point appropriately to get the right diversity? Can you actually go beyond what the base model can generate? Are some things more likely than the others, in which case can we correct that in some way? What if we want to generate more of one kind than the other? All of these things are still going to be quite challenging with the current paradigm. Hopefully if we do pre-training in a way that allows this kind of diverse, controlled sampling, then there's more that we can get.

The thing that's basically unclear is: how do we get that diversity, and how do we actually span things? If we just let it all be end to end from the model, then there might be some collapse, and the model might not be generating all the diverse things that we need. Some of that you can simulate by carefully collecting training data. But if you want to do stuff that's very different from your training data, how do all of these things work? That's hard to say. What we're saying is that we want the model to try a new idea and then stick to it, rather than introducing randomness at every step.

items.answer: In our toy settings, there's no notion of a prompt. I guess there's no instruction, but you can think of that as prepend. items.question: How do you see improvements in base-model sampling contributing to reinforcement learning training?
items.object: Base-model sampling improvements for reinforcement learning
items.answer:
Yeah, this is fascinating. I think overall any improvements that we can do to the base model in terms of how we sample, that directly translates to RL, because a lot of the RL is you try a bunch of things from the model and you make the model do more of what it's doing well. If you just have better starting points, then you will automatically improve all of these things.

The way I think a lot of this could be useful is in ideas like structured exploration and so on. People keep bringing up that exploration is one of the biggest challenges of the next frontier. If we want to do structured exploration over many different spaces, the more control you have over the kind of diversity, the better. I feel like that's very compatible and would actually be really useful for further adult training.

items.question: How do you think language models should be designed to stay up to date?
items.object: Keeping language models updated
items.answer:
I think we really want to scale up a lot of these things, both for ourselves but also to convince people that these are the interventions that are worth investing in for training their future models. Especially this adaptability part: I often think, how do people keep their models fresh? Right now we're at a point where everyone is training new models every year, and maybe we haven't thought about this issue. At some point we're not going to be able to do that.

The answer here is just do retrieval. That gets you their latest facts and everything's okay. We had this other paper that was an oral at the previous conference where we show how models are not going to be that good at using the context and overriding their parametric information. This is not really a magic solution to keeping the models updated. I feel like the aspect that's really interesting to think about is how do we actually make models that are easy to update? What's the right way to decompose or disentangle these aspects of what should be preserved and what should be updated?

items.question: What excites you about improving diversity and creative generation in LLMs for scientific applications?
items.object: Diversity and creative exploration in LLMs for scientific applications
items.answer: I'm really excited about scaling up these ideas for improving diversity and creative generations. We're looking at things like theorem proving and trying to build systems that help mathematicians. Every time I talk to people who want to use LLMs, I keep coming back to: how do we make sure models can actually search and find creative things, for example finding counterexamples? We can use LLMs; they would be great, but how do we ensure they find that kind of structured exploration, finding creative counterexamples? I would be very excited about using these ideas in all of these different applications that are top of mind for people right now, in terms of interesting applications that can push the frontiers across various notions of science.
